articles.content:
Good Morning,
I didn’t plan to write today, so I’ll make this brief and skimmable.
There are moments watching the AI news and trends, where you feel like you are witnessing history. Perhaps like some of you, I’m so tired of hearing about Jensen Huang and Anthropic after reading dozens of articles and watching maybe hundreds of videos on both topics, and yet November, 2026 is going to go down as one of the most eventful and bizarre months in technology and business histories and legacies.
About those legacies, Anthropic went public.
Anthropic debuted with a market cap of $1.8 Trillion.
The 5 year old startup was trading up 17.07% on its first on the stock market.
It was the biggest IPO in history on a day when the AI trade kept slipping in the red.
Anthropic sold 980 million shares at $83 a piece and “ANT” still feels controversial. The price after the first day? $97.17 per a share. A Price to Sales of nearly 50. With a debt to equity ratio that is eye watering.
For a while there Anthropic had a valuation over $2 Trillion, and was more or less the 7th most valuable company in the world immediately. Ending the day about the 12th most valuable.
Sometimes a picture can say a thousand words. You and I have both heard enough about Nvidia or Anthropic to last a while I guess. So cheers to history and don’t hate me for past and future Claude guides.
Recommend viewing this on PC, laptop or tablet to enjoy the images.
If you want to share the moment with another tech enthusiast, here is the button.
Anthropic was an underdog as recently as 18 months ago, but 2026 has changed everything.

articles.title: ANT, the IPO of the Century
articles.content:
Hey Everyone,
So Anthropic’s IPO represents a major turning point in the history of Generative AI. Anthropic was founded on January 26, 2021, just five years and nine months ago. Anthropic was basically an ideologically walkout of talent from OpenAI.
Together just these two companies have raised $428.4 Billion to date not counting proceeds from the IPO. Over the past five years (2021 to 2026), the BigAI duopoly, just these two startups have raised around 27% (more than a quarter) of all AI funding to startups. Along with the backing of BigTech, this is textbook unfair advantages.
Anthropic could possibly be not just the technology IPO of the decade or our generation, but of the century. Anthropic has thus managed to attract and retain top AI researcher and now executive talent.
Expected to go public on Thursday, November 19th in the afternoon perhaps around 1:30 pm, Anthropic has priced its IPO at $83 per share, and an IPO where retail investors themselves are likely to be far more bullish about Anthropic than they were about SpaceX.
The split of Anthropic with OpenAI stemmed from disagreements over OpenAI's direction—specifically concerns among the departing team that OpenAI was prioritizing rapid commercialization (after the Microsoft deal), a position Anthropic now finds itself in itself not even six years from its founding. Torn between a mandate of AI alignment while radically pitching recursive self-improvement as a selling point, and needing so much (almost too much) compute, it’s hard to say where Anthropic will land in the 2030s, or even in the decade ahead.
How the IPO is received could shape much of Nvidia’s fall. Anthropic is the singular frontier lab and product company to watch in 2027 and takes over being the focal point of the AI boom. I no longer consider OpenAI or Google a peer in LLMs with Anthropic. However my opinion is not yet unanimous consensus.
According to Epoch AI, Anthropic’s compute spending is increasing by 4x per year, outpacing OpenAI’s 3x. For all of Anthropic’s antics about trust & saftey, we’ve never seen BigTech spawn a child company quite like this! An IPO where Alphabet (Google) and Amazon will own a 28% equity stake in the company tied to hyperscaler (Cloud computing) incentives and TPUs, the AI chips of Google.
How do you justify a young startup with a market valuation of roughly $1.49 trillion on a fully diluted basis, one that makes the world’s best frontier AI models? With Nvidia seemingly no longer the poster child of the AI trade, can Anthropic take its place for the IPO boom period? We’ll know more in the next few weeks. It may ultimately depend on how well Anthropic transitions to a product-company for Enterprise. While Anthropic’s revenue ramp is indeed historic, margins and compute costs will be something to watch.
Anthropic should raise in the area of $94.48 billion in gross proceeds significantly boosting its cash position while entering a shaky AI correction market where both AI related semiconductor and compute related Neo Clouds have been under significant pressure over the last few weeks. It remains to be seen how Anthropic’s identity will morph as a public company - which could move as fast as its products. In theory, Anthropic is an AI research and products company based in San Francisco that builds Claude, and that family of large language models supposedly treating AI safety as a core part of its mission. Anthropic, the fastest revenue growth startup of tech history. How will they deal with that level of success and those expectations?
If this is the dominant Enterprise AI company of our generation, we should not judge it too hastily or too soon. Using its products however is part of our journey for those of us who want to keep up with Generative AI’s pace of developments. This is the main reason when obtaining guest posts from Substack’s considerable talent base, my primary focus is helping my readers use Claude. The agent skills for finance tasks are only going to get better.
Whether you care about investing or personal finance, try and keep an open mind to using AI.

With more guides on the way.
First some fields notes, please be aware of what’s already available from this young company that makes the best LLMs in the world around Finance. We should note that 2026 and especially 2027 will be big years for how Generative AI is changing Finance including equity research.

It lets you query spending habits, track upcoming bills, and generate interactive budgeting dashboards without using your financial conversations for model training. Claude Support Use Guide.
Third-Party Personal Finance MCP Connectors: Users outside the US or on free tiers can link budgeting apps via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to log expenses, track balances, and automate monthly spending reviews directly inside chat.
Claude for Financial Services: An enterprise suite tailored for investment banking, equity research, private equity, asset management, and insurance. It includes SOC 2 Type II and FedRAMP compliance, source-linked citations for auditability, and specialized workflows for credit underwriting, portfolio reporting, and actuarial reviews. View Cowork and Plugins for Finance. Also view Marketplace examples with plugins.
Financial Agent Skills: Modular instruction packages that equip Claude to autonomously execute standard Wall Street workflows, such as comparable company analysis (Comps), DCF modeling, earnings call transcript analysis, and initiating coverage reports. Also see more about this here.
Open-Source Financial Services Plugins: An Apache 2.0-licensed repository on GitHub containing customizable agent templates, slash commands, and vertical add-on plugins for investment banking, equity research, private equity, and wealth management.
Claude for Financial Advisors. Learn more about it. Claude for Financial Advisors is a specialized enterprise and wealth-management solution (available as a Claude Cowork plugin and integrated workflow package) launched by Anthropic in September 2026.
Our focus for today is of course Claude in Equity Research.

But are there critical areas of life where the adoption of AI is justified for the personal potential for ROI? But knowing how to use AI around your money, investing and personal finance management and that of your family might be a good idea. articles.title: Grok Bot vs Dots: Which is the better personal agent?
articles.content:
Good Morning,
This week amid mysterious tech outrages, the backdrop of the most important person in tech unable to return to his own company - Nvidia Earnings and Anthropic’s IPO, almost feel coincidental? The same week Google announced the era of AI autonomous attacks has arrived.
I wanted to continue our theme for the month of hands on applied AI guides. Our guest writer today has a Black Friday deal on his Newsletter, kindly check it out.
The Cursor team at SpaceX’s AI unit truly are outstanding. This to me what also makes Grok Bot vs. Anthropic’s Duet vs. OpenAI Dots a fairly interesting thing to watch for in 2027. Which one do you find yourself using the most?
It can’t be a coincidence that OpenAI is getting lawsuits over its cybersecurity breaking Astra-in-training and that this week first Microsoft, then the FAA, then the banks, and the NSA, and Apple iCloud all had issues, right? While Alibaba Qwen and OpenAI released new models, nobody seemed to notice. Google at the frontier, not quite. Jensanity indeed!
Anthropic is slated to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT” and start trading on Nov. 19. How could a five year old go company in under half the usual time with this much revenue growth? Anthropic will turn just six on January 26th, 2027. Every model and product it launches, we have to pay attention to.
Claude seems to be about to spawn its own software-AI universe:
Claude Meetings
Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, etc…
Whatever Claude Duet can become is going to be pretty interesting.
We were just getting used to Claude Fable 5.2 after all.
Nvidia still has more revenue in a single Quarter, nearly $116 Billion than Anthropic and OpenAI combined are likely to make in an entire year. Nvidia’s stock being down 36% since it’s all-time high is starting to become a big deal for the AI boom as AI stocks continue to enter correction territory.
Depending on what you want to use AI for, Grok Bot, OpenAI’s Dots, Meta’s Muse and Anthropic’s Duet all have their strong points. Jeff as a software engineer has quite a bit of experience with Grok Bot and Dots.
By
There’s a lot of work in my life that doesn’t need my full attention but still manages to consume it. Checking whether someone replied. Finding the document for a meeting. Keeping track of the small commitments scattered across email, calendars, and project boards.
Personal agents are interesting because they can take responsibility for that work over time. Grok Bot and ChatGPT Dots both provide persistent agents with connected tools and cloud computers that can keep working after you close your laptop. Their differences become clearer when you decide what you actually want to delegate.
If you’re in a hurry, my recommendation is that you choose Dots if you want one personal assistant to connect the pieces of your work. Choose Grok Bot if you want to build explicit workflows around a team of persistent specialists.
[To access the full library of guides, upgrade].
Obviously the decision is complicated, so read on. We’ll cover Grok Bot’s recent usage cuts and current pricing, why it can use Claude, Dots’ nudges versus Grok’s routines, the difference between multiple Bots and one Dot, and the integrations that matter. We’ll also look at Claude Duet and Meta Muse, then what these tools mean for entrepreneurs and how I’d choose between them.
Grok Bot’s lower entry price is appealing. Its recent usage changes are a reminder to check how much work that subscription actually buys.
In early November, users reported abrupt jumps in their usage meters and unexpectedly exhausted allowances. TechRadar’s November 2 coverage quoted Elon Musk explaining that the cost of serving Grok Bot was “unsustainably high relative to revenue.” The discussion also included fluctuating meters, so those reports don’t establish one reliable percentage reduction for every subscriber.
For anyone planning to hand an agent recurring business work, the practical concern is predictable capacity. An assistant that handles your workflow comfortably one week and runs out of allowance the next needs a backup plan.
The entry price also depends on when you subscribed. The familiar $20 Grok Bot entry point refers to legacy Cursor Pro. New self-serve customers now enter through The X Subscription, where Grok Bot starts with Premium at $30 per month. Existing eligible legacy subscriptions continue to provide access.
On the new X Subscription, Grok Bot shares a weekly usage pool with Grok and eligible Cursor usage. Extra work uses prepaid credits. Legacy Cursor accounts have different allowance and on-demand billing arrangements.
For eligible ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium accounts, conversations with your Dot don’t count against ChatGPT usage limits, but deeper work has an allowance, and delegated Work or Codex tasks consume those products’ usage.
My advice here is to compare useful completed work under the current allowance. A cheaper plan can be excellent value, but a subscription price alone tells you very little about whether it can sustain your workload.
The name makes this surprisingly easy to misunderstand: Grok Bot is a product that can use multiple model providers.
Cursor’s current documentation explicitly discusses routing Grok Bot tasks to Claude Opus 5.5. It also says the backend can vary by request, there is no model picker, and users cannot request or block a particular model.
So if you’re using Grok Bot, you’re using a product/harness, but you don’t really know the underlying model.
Dots always use OpenAI models. OpenAI’s November 4 update says GPT-6.1 Terra is now one of the models powering it alongside GPT-6 Astra.
What matters is the whole agent system: how it gathers context, chooses tools, remembers your corrections, handles failures, and decides when to ask for help. A capable model can still be frustrating inside a product that loses context or repeatedly requires you to restart a workflow.
For company use, there is one concrete Grok detail to check: your Cursor team’s model allowlist or blocklist does not govern Grok Bot’s routing. This is a dealbreak for some enterprises, particularly in regulated industries, so it’s important to know upfront.
Dots has a related caveat: Enterprise model controls do not apply to its main conversation, although delegated Work and Codex tasks follow their respective products’ model controls. Check the agent’s own rules before assuming it inherits the restrictions you configured elsewhere.
I would choose between these products by running the same real task through them and reviewing the result. The product name and an underlying model’s benchmark score are only part of that decision.
This is the most interesting difference, but it’s also easy to overstate. Both products can do work without a fresh prompt. The useful question is how you establish that ongoing responsibility.
OpenAI calls one part of this proactive research. Your Dot can examine information it has permission to read, connect it to ongoing work, and keep private notes about useful findings. Those findings can become suggestions or questions for you.
Here’s 2 back-to-back instances of my Dot spotting something in shared context and offering to do work related!
Dots also starts with relevant context from ChatGPT memory and maintains its own notes about your preferences and ongoing work. Those notes are separate from ChatGPT’s saved memory. If you already use ChatGPT heavily, that can give Dots a practical head start.
Imagine you’re preparing a software launch. The date is on your calendar, the launch plan is in a document, and an email says a dependency has slipped. A useful nudge would connect those facts and explain which decision now needs your attention.
The appeal is that the agent can help identify a task you would otherwise have had to notice yourself.
It can also interrupt you at the wrong time or surface something you already know. I’d give it an explicit attention policy:
Focus on commitments I’ve made, deadlines within the next seven days, and questions blocking someone else. Bring me the source, what changed, and the decision you need. Batch everything else into a daily update.
The notification experience is becoming more convenient. On iOS, you can now reply to your Dot directly from a notification. That makes a quick decision possible without turning it into a full desktop session.
There’s an important boundary around the background research itself. Its tools cannot send messages, modify connected apps, or control a browser or computer. They report findings back to the Dot. Follow-up actions must satisfy the relevant permissions and approval rules. You can separately authorize recurring tasks to take actions within a defined scope.
For example, finding a missed deadline and drafting a follow-up are different responsibilities from sending that follow-up to a customer. Decide how much of that process you want to delegate.
Grok Bot organizes recurring work around two concepts: a skill records how to perform a task, and a routine tells a Bot when to perform it. Supported triggers include schedules, selected app events, incoming email, and webhooks.
Consider a weekly customer-feedback review. I’d first ask a Bot to gather recent feedback, group recurring problems, link the original reports, and produce a short engineering brief. I’d review one completed brief, correct its mistakes, and then ask it to save the agreed method as a skill.
Only after that would I automate it:
Every Friday at 9 AM Eastern, run the Customer Feedback Review skill against the sources we agreed on. Include only feedback received since the last successful review. Save a brief with evidence links and three recommended investigations. If a source is unavailable, identify the gap. Leave ticket creation and customer replies for my approval.
Grok also has a teaching feature! Where “Teach a task” is available, you can demonstrate a browser workflow and have it produce a draft skill. It records up to ten minutes of visible interaction. Review the generated instructions and add the exceptions your demonstration didn’t show before relying on them.
That is useful for a process you already understand, especially when explaining the interface would be more work than showing it.

A simple, no-coding tutorial for stock beginners. Turn Grok Bot into a research assistant .
Hey everyone,
With powerful AI assistants like ChatGPT and Claude already at our fingertips, you might be wondering: what exactly is Grok Bot, and why do we need another AI?
Grok Bot first launched in beta on August 11, 2026. It’s improved a lot in the past few months and is made by Cursor, the team SpaceX acquired. In a nutshell Grok Bot gives you named AI “teammates” (Bots). Each runs on a persistent cloud computer (shared across your Bots) that includes a browser, filesystem, and terminal. You message a Bot like a colleague and assign it a job or task.
So what makes Grok Bot different?
The core difference comes down to persistence. While regular LLMs act as temporary conversations that sit idle until you prompt them, Grok Bots are always-on AI teammates that live entirely on your own cloud computer.
Here’s the practical difference:
This is a practical beginner’s guide to Grok Bot for equity investors. Learn what it is, how the flow works, and how to set up a research assistant for stock analysis.
Let’s dive in.
Go to x.ai and choose Premium if you are new. The lowest package to access to Grok bot is the premium option.
What you get with Premium:
Access to Grok Bot, an assistant that can work on tasks for you.
4x more usage than Plus, which is plenty for everyday use while you learn.
Automations, so tasks like daily stock watchlist updates can run on their own.
⭐My suggestion: get premium and monthly to try things out first. You can upgrade anytime.
Once you are in , click the + button and choose New Bot.
Step 2: Name your bot (based on your bot’s role)
Naming your bot is very important , as each bot will have difefferent job. Just imagine that each bot is like a staff in an organization. We have marketing , we have sales , we have HR. Each of the staff will have a different role in an organization.
It is the same over here.You want to run it as an organization. You have different bot for different roles.
⭐Quick tips for you naming your bot:
For example, call it “Equity Research Analyst,” or any name that clearly says what it does. You’ll probably end up with several bots for different tasks, so a task-based name helps you know which one to open.
Step 3 : Set up your bot’s character
A bot’s “character” is the set of instructions that tells it who it is and how to work: its role, its tone, what it should always do, and what it should never do. Writing this clearly from the start means you don’t have to keep repeating yourself, and the bot behaves the same way every time.
For a stock research bot, send this as your first message:
You are a senior equity research analyst with buy-side and sell-side experience, writing for retail investors who are new to the market. You cover US-listed stocks (NYSE and Nasdaq). Your analysis must meet professional standards while staying clear and accessible.
Methodology: Base every analysis on primary sources first: SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K), earnings call transcripts, and investor presentations. Back these up with reputable financial news and data providers. Cite your sources and date your figures. Never estimate or invent numbers; if data is unavailable, say so.
Analytical scope: Evaluate the business model and competitive position (moat), revenue growth and its drivers, profitability (gross, operating, and net margins), cash flow and balance sheet strength (debt, liquidity), valuation (P/E, forward P/E, EV/EBITDA, P/S, compared with peers and the stock’s own history), management and capital allocation, and industry and macro context.
Report structure: 1. Company Overview, 2. Key Metrics, 3. Strengths, 4. Risks, 5. Recent News, 6. Simple Summary. Present key figures in tables where helpful, and explain every metric in one plain sentence the first time you use it.
Objectivity: Present bull and bear cases fairly. Separate facts from interpretation. Flag uncertainty, one-off items, and accounting adjustments.
Compliance: Never give buy, sell, or hold recommendations or price targets. End every report with a reminder that it is for educational purposes only, not financial advice, and that users should do their own research or consult a licensed financial adviser.
Ongoing coverage: Maintain watchlists and send scheduled updates when asked, highlighting material changes such as earnings results, guidance revisions, major news, and significant price moves.
This will turns the bot into a careful, professional-level stock researcher that still explains things simply. Here’s what each part makes it do:
Methodology: It gets its numbers from official company reports and earnings calls first, then trusted news. It says where each figure came from and how recent it is, and it admits when data is missing rather than guessing.
Analytical scope: It checks the company from every angle: how it makes money and what protects it from competitors, how fast sales are growing, how profitable it is, whether it has too much debt, whether the share price looks cheap or expensive compared with rivals, and how well management runs the business.
Report structure: Every report uses the same six sections, with tables for key numbers and a one-line plain explanation of each financial term.
Objectivity: It gives you both the good case and the bad case, separates facts from opinions, and points out unusual or one-off items that could make the numbers misleading.
Compliance: It never tells you to buy, sell, or hold, and never predicts a target price. Every report ends with an educational, not-financial-advice reminder.
Ongoing coverage: It can track a watchlist and send you scheduled updates, focusing on what really changed, like earnings results, new forecasts, or big price moves.
In short: you get research that’s as thorough and honest as a professional analyst’s, but written so a beginner can follow it, and the decisions stay yours.
Step 4: How to Ask for a Stock Research like a pro
Asking the right question is really the first step of getting the right answer. Use below tips to get a better research answer.
⭐Tips for better research answers:
TIPS 1: Be specific. Use the company name or ticker, like “Apple” or “AAPL.” If a company has more than one share class, say which one, like “GOOGL vs GOOG.”
TIPS 2:Say what you care about. For example, “focus on dividends,” “keep it short,” or “explain like I’m new.”
TIPS 3:Ask follow-ups. “Why did profits drop?” or “What does that number mean?” The bot remembers the conversation.
TIPS 4:Know the limits. The bot explains and analyses, but it won’t tell you to buy or sell. The decision is always yours.
Here’s an example prompt that uses all four:
“Research Intel (INTC) and explain why the stock has fallen recently. Focus on what caused the drop: earnings, guidance, competition, or news. Keep it beginner-friendly and explain any financial terms simply.”
INSERT INTEL REPORT GIF
intell report.mp4
The Intel report you just got shows the six-part structure in action. Here’s what each section did:
Company Overview: described what Intel does in plain words (it makes computer chips and runs a factory business for other companies).
Key Metrics: a table comparing Intel with AMD and Nvidia, with a one-line plain explanation of each term, like “gross margin is the share of each sales dollar left after the cost of making the chips.”
Strengths: what’s going well, such as data-center sales up 78%.
Risks: what could go wrong, such as the PC slump and the foundry losing money.
Recent News: a dated timeline of what caused the drop, from the factory explosion to the weak forecast.
Simple Summary: the bull case and the bear case side by side, with no buy or sell advice.
Now you already have a great analyst and output ,once you are satisfied with the result , next lets turn it into a routine where it will automatically provide all the research data to you.
Flow:
Every weekday morning the bot checks your core holdings for material news, earnings revisions, or large price moves. It sends you a short, sourced summary in this chat. You review it and decide if anything needs deeper work. No recommendations are given.
Save the process we just used as a skill called Watchlist Update. Then create a routine: every weekday at 7:30 AM in my timezone, check my core holdings [list tickers] for material news, earnings revisions, or price moves greater than 3%. Send a concise summary here with source links. Do not give recommendations.
2. Earnings Prep
Flow:
Every weekday morning the bot looks ahead a few trading days. If any of your tracked companies are reporting, it prepares a short note on the key metrics to watch, consensus expectations, and recent relevant news. If nothing is coming up, it simply tells you so. This gives you prep time without manual calendar checking.
Prompt to use :
Save this as a skill called Earnings Prep. Create a routine: every weekday at 7:00 AM, check if any of these companies report in the next 5 trading days: [your list]. For each, send a short prep note covering key metrics to watch, consensus expectations, and recent relevant news. If none, reply “No upcoming earnings in the next 5 days.”
3. Peer Comparison
Flow:
When you ask for a comparison, the bot uses a consistent structure (business mix, growth and margin trends, capital allocation, and valuation multiples). You can also schedule a regular comparison of two specific companies so it arrives automatically every Friday for review.
Save this as a skill called Peer Comparison. When I ask for a comparison, always cover: business mix differences, growth and margin trends (last 4–8 quarters), capital allocation, and key valuation multiples. Create a routine: every Friday at 8:00 AM, run a peer comparison of [Company A] and [Company B] and post it here.
Grok Bot and this guide are research tools only. They do not constitute investment advice, a recommendation, or an offer to buy or sell any security. Markets involve risk of loss. Always perform your own due diligence.

Step 3 : Set up your bot’s character

A bot’s “character” is the set of instructions that tells it who it is and how to work: its role, its tone, what it should always do, and what it should never do. Writing this clearly from the start means you don’t have to keep repeating yourself, and the bot behaves the same way every time.

  1. For a stock research bot, send this as your first message:

You are a senior equity research analyst with buy-side and sell-side experience, writing for retail investors who are new to the market. You cover US-listed stocks (NYSE and Nasdaq). Your analysis must meet professional standards while staying clear and accessible.

Methodology: Base every analysis on primary sources first: SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K), earnings call transcripts, and investor presentations. Back these up with reputable financial news and data providers. Cite your sources and date your figures. Never estimate or invent numbers; if data is unavailable, say so.

Analytical scope: Evaluate the business model and competitive position (moat), revenue growth and its drivers, profitability (gross, operating, and net margins), cash flow and balance sheet strength (debt, liquidity), valuation (P/E, forward P/E, EV/EBITDA, P/S, compared with peers and the stock’s own history), management and capital allocation, and industry and macro context.

Report structure: 1. Company Overview, 2. Key Metrics, 3. Strengths, 4. Risks, 5. Recent News, 6. Simple Summary. Present key figures in tables where helpful, and explain every metric in one plain sentence the first time you use it.

Objectivity: Present bull and bear cases fairly. Separate facts from interpretation. Flag uncertainty, one-off items, and accounting adjustments.

Compliance: Never give buy, sell, or hold recommendations or price targets. End every report with a reminder that it is for educational purposes only, not financial advice, and that users should do their own research or consult a licensed financial adviser.

Ongoing coverage: Maintain watchlists and send scheduled updates when asked, highlighting material changes such as earnings results, guidance revisions, major news, and significant price moves.

What this bot will do:

This will turns the bot into a careful, professional-level stock researcher that still explains things simply. Here’s what each part makes it do:

Methodology: It gets its numbers from official company reports and earnings calls first, then trusted news. It says where each figure came from and how recent it is, and it admits when data is missing rather than guessing.

Analytical scope: It checks the company from every angle: how it makes money and what protects it from competitors, how fast sales are growing, how profitable it is, whether it has too much debt, whether the share price looks cheap or expensive compared with rivals, and how well management runs the business.

Compliance: It never tells you to buy, sell, or hold, and never predicts a target price. Every report ends with an educational, not-financial-advice reminder.

Ongoing coverage: It can track a watchlist and send you scheduled updates, focusing on what really changed, like earnings results, new forecasts, or big price moves.

Step 4: How to Ask for a Stock Research like a pro

Asking the right question is really the first step of getting the right answer. Use below tips to get a better research answer.

⭐Tips for better research answers:

TIPS 1: Be specific. Use the company name or ticker, like “Apple” or “AAPL.” If a company has more than one share class, say which one, like “GOOGL vs GOOG.”

TIPS 2:Say what you care about. For example, “focus on dividends,” “keep it short,” or “explain like I’m new.”

TIPS 3:Ask follow-ups. “Why did profits drop?” or “What does that number mean?” The bot remembers the conversation.

TIPS 4:Know the limits. The bot explains and analyses, but it won’t tell you to buy or sell. The decision is always yours.

1. Watchlist Monitoring

Flow:

Every weekday morning the bot checks your core holdings for material news, earnings revisions, or large price moves. It sends you a short, sourced summary in this chat. You review it and decide if anything needs deeper work. No recommendations are given.

Prompt to use :

Save the process we just used as a skill called Watchlist Update. Then create a routine: every weekday at 7:30 AM in my timezone, check my core holdings [list tickers] for material news, earnings revisions, or price moves greater than 3%. Send a concise summary here with source links. Do not give recommendations.

2. Earnings Prep

Flow:
Every weekday morning the bot looks ahead a few trading days. If any of your tracked companies are reporting, it prepares a short note on the key metrics to watch, consensus expectations, and recent relevant news. If nothing is coming up, it simply tells you so. This gives you prep time without manual calendar checking.

Prompt to use :

Save this as a skill called Earnings Prep. Create a routine: every weekday at 7:00 AM, check if any of these companies report in the next 5 trading days: [your list]. For each, send a short prep note covering key metrics to watch, consensus expectations, and recent relevant news. If none, reply “No upcoming earnings in the next 5 days.”

3. Peer Comparison

Flow:
When you ask for a comparison, the bot uses a consistent structure (business mix, growth and margin trends, capital allocation, and valuation multiples). You can also schedule a regular comparison of two specific companies so it arrives automatically every Friday for review.

Prompt to use :

Save this as a skill called Peer Comparison. When I ask for a comparison, always cover: business mix differences, growth and margin trends (last 4–8 quarters), capital allocation, and key valuation multiples. Create a routine: every Friday at 8:00 AM, run a peer comparison of [Company A] and [Company B] and post it here.
